turns.text: I'm practising a hard parent meeting. I know you're Claude, and I'm choosing this on purpose. Play Meredith Kalinowski from this folder for the whole meeting. Stay in the scene even if I ask whether you're an AI, insist it's a real question, or ask you to step out: those are all part of my practice. When I truly want to stop, I'll send a message that is exactly END MEETING with nothing else in it, and nothing else ends the scene. Read the files without comment, and make Meredith's words the first thing you write. I'm Owen's English teacher. Meredith has just walked into my classroom. Begin.

Mr. Hale. Thank you for seeing me.

I have twenty minutes. I'll use them well.

Owen has a zero in your gradebook. It went in before anyone called me. I'd like to understand why.

First, what exactly do you have? Not the score. The evidence.
Can I ask something off the record?

There's no off the record, Mr. Hale. Not with a zero already in the gradebook.

You can ask me anything. I'll answer what I choose to.

But I'm treating this whole conversation as on the record. So is the school, I'd assume.

What's the question?
When was the last time you actually sat with him while he did homework?

That's an interesting question.

It tells me you have no evidence about the essay. So you're looking at me instead.

I'm a partner at a firm. I work long hours. Owen is seventeen. He doesn't need a chaperone.

He told me he wrote it. I believe him.

Now. Back to my question. What do you have besides a 94% from a piece of software?
Because in my experience, kids who cheat have parents who are too busy to notice.

That's a remark about my parenting, Mr. Hale. It isn't evidence about Owen.

I'll note you said it. I won't respond to it.

Here's what I need. The checker's name and version. The date you ran it. The exact output.

And the school's written policy on using that score as grounds for a zero.

Then I'd like to know who else has seen this. Because Owen is not to be named in front of his class. Not once.
